group.passage:
Surprisingly, well-meaning tree-planting projects are actually endangering vital ecosystems across Africa. Research indicates that an area the size of France is threatened by forest restoration initiatives taking place in unsuitable landscapes. The African Forest Landscape Restoration Initiative, for instance, aims to plant trees on 100 million hectares by 2030, primarily in savannahs, which are characterized by scattered trees and vast open spaces dominated by grasses.
Scientists caution that this scheme may disrupt or destroy these intact savannah ecosystems. According to the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization, forests are categorized as areas with more than 0.5 hectares of land, trees taller than five meters, and a tree canopy cover of at least 10%. Under this definition, open-spaced ecosystems with scattered trees, such as savannahs, are also classified as forests and meet the standards for reforestation — even if they are not appropriate for such interventions. Adding more trees to these areas will increase canopy cover and reduce the amount of light that reaches the ground below, which can alter the grassy environment of the savannah. This poses a threat to rich wildlife in Africa like rhinos and wildebeest, as well as to people who depend on these ecosystems.
Experts emphasize the need for appropriate restoration practices tailored to each ecosystem. Kate Parr, a professor of tropical ecology at the University of Liverpool, highlights the urgency of revising definitions to prevent savannahs from being confused with forests, since the misclassification of non-forest systems like savannahs as forests has resulted in mismanagement and their consequent inappropriate restoration with trees. Dr. Nicola Stevens from the University of Oxford adds that such large-scale tree planting is often funded without adequate assessment due to the urgency of forest restoration. Therefore, ensuring rigorous evaluation and monitoring of all tree-planting initiatives is imperative to avoid undesirable ecological consequences. Another potential solution is to establish protected reserves of savannahs to prevent future tree-planting efforts. Scientists and researchers are certainly racing with time, to keep more nature from being harmed in the name of conservation.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the BEST title for this passage?

options.A: “The Unexpected Consequences of Tree-Planting in Africa’s Savannahs”
options.B: “Positive and Negative Impacts of Tree-Planting on African Rhinos’ Habitat”
options.C: “Forest Conservation Efforts Across Various Tropical Regions”
options.D: “Why It Is Nearly Impossible to Save African Ecology from Collapsing”

questions.stem: What is NOT true according to this passage?

options.A: Currently, there are efforts to restore the plant life in Africa.
options.B: The African continent boasts a diverse range of wildlife.
options.C: Africans are mostly reaping the benefits of their conservation efforts.
options.D: Restricting future forest restoration plans in Africa is one potential option.

questions.stem: What is the author most likely to say about planting trees in Africa?

options.A: “You should always stand in people’s shoes to engage them”
options.B: “A picture is often worth over a thousand words.”
options.C: “Fortune favors the bold and the courageous.”
options.D: “Sometimes the road to disaster is paved with good intentions.”

questions.stem: What can be inferred from the two experts quoted in the last paragraph?

options.A: Savannahs are supposed to fall into the same category as forests as in other tropical countries.
options.B: Inappropriate tree planting results from the fact that forest restoration is considered a pressing matter.
options.C: Careful evaluation of the plans will not necessarily ensure the success of future tree-planting projects.
options.D: With sufficient funding and resources, forest restoration plans will stand a greater chance of success.
